objective: Configuring a SOHO network: static vs. DHCP addressing, NAT, firewall rules, and port forwarding
secondaryObjectives: Configuring and troubleshooting VPN, VLAN, and QoS settings on a SOHO router
Wireless standards and encryption: 802.11 generations, frequency bands, and WPA2/WPA3

sources.cite: CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) V15: domains Mobile devices 13%, Networking 23%, Hardware 25%, Virtualization and cloud computing 11%, Hardware and network troubleshooting 28%; launched 2025-03-25
sources.note: Exam page read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-14 ('Diagnosing issues: identifying and fixing hardware, network, and connectivity problems'). The objectives PDF (Exam Objectives Version 1.2) was read in primary text the same day: 5.5 'Given a scenario, troubleshoot network issues' lists 'Limited connectivity' and 'Intermittent internet connectivity'; 2.6 lists APIPA, static and dynamic addressing, subnet mask and gateway; 2.4 lists DHCP leases, reservations, scope and exclusions. The PDF says the troubleshooting methodology 'will not be tested' in the 220-1200 series but remains a competency standard. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's rogue-dhcp-soho-office (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

The business, the users, the devices and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You support Brightsmile Dental, a fictional two-chair dental office. The owner wants to watch the waiting-room camera from home, patients want Wi-Fi, and the router still has its installer's settings.
handover: The camera gets its address from DHCP; the patient-records PC and the camera share one flat network.
Wi-Fi: one network, WPA2 with a password printed at the front desk.
howItWorks: The desk shows the ticket queue against the priority matrix and each service's status.
Move on a ticket round at a time. A decision comes to you at each ticket round; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Round 2: the camera is taken over by a botnet within a day and starts scanning the office network.
Round 3: a patient's infected laptop spreads malware to the records PC over the shared network.
Round 4: someone in the car park joins the open office network and browses the shared folders.

camPrompt.title: Reach the camera from home
camPrompt.context: The owner wants to see the waiting room from home.

choices.label: Give the camera a DHCP reservation, change its default password, and let the owner reach it through the router's VPN rather than a forwarded port

effects.log: The camera has a fixed address and is reached only over the VPN.

choices.feedback: A reservation keeps the address stable; the VPN gives remote access without opening the camera to the internet.

choices.label: Reserve its address and forward port 8080 to it after changing the password

effects.log: Port 8080 is forwarded to the camera.

choices.feedback: It works, but the camera's web interface is now open to the whole internet.

choices.label: Put the camera in the router's DMZ and keep the default password

effects.log: The camera is in the DMZ with the default password.

choices.feedback: A DMZ host receives every unsolicited connection; with the default password it is taken over in hours.

guestPrompt.title: Patients on the same network as records
guestPrompt.context: The router supports a guest network on its own VLAN.

choices.label: Turn on the guest network on its own VLAN with client isolation and no access to the LAN, a separate password, and a bandwidth limit

effects.log: Guests are on their own VLAN with no LAN access.

choices.feedback: A guest VLAN keeps patients' devices away from the records PC.

choices.label: Tell patients there is no Wi-Fi
choices.feedback: Safe, but the owner asked for it and patients will ask staff for their password.

choices.label: Keep giving patients the office Wi-Fi password

effects.log: Patients keep using the office network.

choices.feedback: Every patient device can reach the records PC.

wpaPrompt.title: WPA2 with a printed password
wpaPrompt.context: All office devices support WPA3; the router supports WPA3 and a WPA2/WPA3 transition mode.

choices.label: Switch to WPA3-Personal (transition mode only if an old device needs it), set a new long passphrase known only to staff, and turn off WPS

effects.log: WPA3 with a new staff-only passphrase; WPS off.

choices.feedback: WPA3 resists offline password guessing; a new passphrase removes everyone who learned the old one.

choices.label: Keep WPA2 and change the password
choices.feedback: Better, but WPA3 was available and stronger.

choices.label: Remove the password so the cameras and card readers connect more easily
choices.feedback: An open network lets anyone nearby join and read unencrypted traffic.

expertPath.text: Read the router's configuration and the camera's options first.
Reserve the camera's address, change its password, reach it over the VPN.
Put guests on an isolated guest VLAN with its own password.
Move to WPA3 with a new staff-only passphrase and WPS off.

camHarm.headline: Don't expose devices
camHarm.body: Reserve the address and reach the device over a VPN; never put it in the DMZ with defaults.

guestHarm.body: A guest VLAN with isolation keeps visitors off the office network.

wpaHarm.body: Use WPA3 with a strong passphrase; never leave the office network open.

scoring.modelReasoning: On a SOHO router, a DHCP reservation gives a device a stable address. Port forwarding and especially the DMZ expose a device to the internet; a VPN gives remote access without that. Guests belong on an isolated guest network or VLAN. WPA3 is stronger than WPA2, a new passphrase removes everyone who knew the old one, and WPS should be off.
